module_title: Business Management for Briquette and Pellet Producers

lessons.title: Calculating Costs: Raw Materials, Labor, Transport, and Packaging
lessons.body: To run a profitable briquette or pellet business, you must know exactly how much it costs to produce one kilogram or one bag. Start by listing all your costs for a typical month. Raw materials: if you buy charcoal dust from a sawmill, you might pay 50,000 UGX per tonne. If you collect agricultural waste like rice husks for free, you still need to account for your time and transport. For a tonne of briquettes, you might need 1.2 tonnes of raw material due to losses. Labor: if you pay 3 workers 10,000 UGX each per day to produce 500 kg, that's 30,000 UGX per day, or 60 UGX per kg. Transport: if you hire a pickup to deliver 1 tonne of briquettes 10 km, it might cost 30,000 UGX, adding 30 UGX per kg. Packaging: a 5 kg bag costs 500 UGX, so 100 UGX per kg. Binder: cassava starch might cost 20,000 UGX per tonne of briquettes, or 20 UGX per kg. Add all these: raw material (50 UGX/kg if 50,000 UGX per tonne), labor (60), transport (30), packaging (100), binder (20) = 260 UGX per kg. But also include fixed costs: rent for your workshop (200,000 UGX per month), machine maintenance (50,000), electricity or fuel (100,000), and your own salary (300,000). If you produce 5,000 kg per month, fixed costs per kg = (200,000+50,000+100,000+300,000)/5,000 = 130 UGX per kg. Total cost per kg = 260 + 130 = 390 UGX. So you must sell above 390 UGX per kg to make a profit. Always recalculate monthly as prices change. Use a notebook or a simple Excel sheet to track these numbers. This is the foundation of your business.

lessons.title: Setting a Profitable Price per Kilogram or Bag
lessons.body: Once you know your cost per kilogram, you can set a price that covers costs and gives you a profit. A common mistake is to look at what competitors charge and just match it, but if your costs are higher, you will lose money. Instead, use a markup. If your total cost is 390 UGX per kg, a 30% markup gives a selling price of 390 x 1.30 = 507 UGX per kg. You might round to 500 UGX per kg for easier selling. For a 5 kg bag, that's 2,500 UGX. But check what the market will bear. In many African cities, charcoal sells for about 1,500 UGX per kg. If your briquettes are cheaper, you can attract customers. However, if your briquettes burn longer, you can charge a premium. For example, if one kg of briquettes replaces 1.5 kg of charcoal, you can price at 1,500 x 1.5 = 2,250 UGX per kg, but that might be too high. A better strategy is to price slightly below charcoal to encourage trials. So if charcoal is 1,500 UGX per kg, price your briquettes at 1,200 UGX per kg. That gives you a profit of 810 UGX per kg (1,200 - 390). But you must also consider volume: lower price might sell more. Do a simple break-even analysis: if your fixed costs are 650,000 UGX per month and you make 810 UGX profit per kg, you need to sell 650,000 / 810 = 803 kg just to cover fixed costs. Anything above that is profit. Test different prices in your market. Offer discounts for bulk purchases, like 10% off for 10 bags or more. Also, consider packaging size: a 2 kg bag might sell for 2,500 UGX (1,250 per kg) because smaller sizes are convenient. Always communicate the value: briquettes are smokeless, burn longer, and save money. Use a simple pricing formula: Price = Cost per kg x (1 + Markup %). Adjust markup based on competition and demand. Review prices every three months.

lessons.title: Keeping Simple Records: Income, Expenses, and Inventory
lessons.body: You cannot manage what you do not measure. Even if you have no formal training, you can keep simple records using a notebook or a free app like Excel on your phone. Start with three columns: Date, Description, and Amount. For income, record every sale: date, customer name (optional), quantity sold (kg or bags), and amount received. For expenses, record every purchase: date, item (e.g., raw materials, labor, transport, packaging), and amount paid. At the end of each day, total your income and expenses. At the end of the month, subtract total expenses from total income to get your profit or loss. Also track inventory: how much raw material you have, how much finished product, and how much packaging. Do a physical count every week. For example, if you started with 1,000 kg of raw material, used 800 kg, you should have 200 kg left. If not, investigate theft or waste. Use a simple inventory sheet: Item, Opening Stock, Added, Used, Closing Stock. For cash, keep a cash box and record every shilling in and out. Never mix business and personal money. If you take money for personal use, record it as 'Owner's Draw' and subtract it from profit. At the end of each month, prepare a simple income statement: Total Sales - Total Expenses = Net Profit. Also prepare a balance sheet: what you own (cash, inventory, equipment) minus what you owe (loans, unpaid bills) = your equity. These records help you get loans, make decisions, and spot problems early. For example, if you see transport costs rising, you can negotiate better rates. Use a separate notebook for each month, and keep all receipts in an envelope. Even a simple exercise book with ruled lines works. The key is consistency: record every transaction immediately.

lessons.title: Managing Cash Flow When Sales Are Seasonal
lessons.body: In many African countries, briquette sales peak during rainy seasons when people need more fuel for cooking and heating, and drop during dry seasons when solar cooking is possible. Or sales might spike during holidays. This seasonality can cause cash shortages. To manage cash flow, first forecast your sales for the next 6-12 months. Look at last year's records: which months were high, which were low? For example, if you sold 5,000 kg in July (rainy) and only 2,000 kg in January (dry), you know to prepare. During high season, maximize production and sales, but set aside cash for low season. A good rule: save 20% of your monthly profit during high season into a separate savings account or mobile money. During low season, use those savings to cover fixed costs like rent and salaries. Also, diversify your products: make both briquettes and pellets, or sell to different markets (households, restaurants, schools). Restaurants need fuel year-round. Another strategy: offer pre-orders or subscriptions. For example, a school might pay monthly for a guaranteed supply of briquettes, giving you steady income. Manage your inventory: during low season, produce less to avoid cash tied up in unsold stock. But keep enough raw materials for unexpected orders. Negotiate with suppliers for credit: buy raw materials now, pay after 30 days. This helps when cash is tight. Also, consider offering discounts for off-season purchases to encourage sales. For example, in dry season, sell a 5 kg bag for 2,200 UGX instead of 2,500 UGX to keep cash coming in. Keep a cash flow budget: list all expected cash inflows and outflows each month. If you see a shortfall, arrange a small loan or use savings. Never run out of cash to pay workers or buy materials. A simple cash flow chart in your notebook can help you see trends.

lessons.title: Hiring and Training Workers for Production
lessons.body: As your briquette business grows, you will need to hire workers. Start by identifying tasks: raw material collection, crushing, mixing, pressing, drying, packaging, and sales. You might do many yourself at first, but when demand exceeds your capacity, hire. For production, you typically need 2-4 workers per shift. When hiring, look for reliability, physical strength, and willingness to learn. You don't need formal education. Pay a fair wage: in many African countries, minimum wage for casual labor is around 10,000-15,000 UGX per day. But to reduce turnover, pay slightly above market, e.g., 12,000 UGX per day, and provide lunch. You can also pay by piece rate: for example, 500 UGX per 5 kg bag produced. This motivates productivity. Train workers on safety: wear masks and gloves when handling dust, operate machines carefully. Show them the correct mix ratio: e.g., 1 part binder to 10 parts raw material. Demonstrate how to operate the press and how to dry briquettes properly (sun-dry for 2-3 days, turn regularly). Use a buddy system: pair a new worker with an experienced one for one week. Keep training simple and hands-on. Also train on quality control: check that briquettes are dense and not crumbling. For sales, hire someone with good communication skills. Pay a base salary plus commission (e.g., 5% of sales) to encourage selling. Keep records of each worker's output and attendance. Use a simple attendance book. Consider hiring women and youth: they are often reliable and can be trained easily. Provide a safe working environment: clean water, shade, and first aid kit. Finally, treat workers with respect. Pay on time, every time. If you cannot pay, communicate early. Happy workers produce more and stay longer.

lessons.title: Accessing Microfinance and Government Grants for Green Businesses
lessons.body: Many briquette producers struggle to get funding from traditional banks because they lack collateral or formal credit history. However, there are options. Microfinance institutions (MFIs) like BRAC, FINCA, and Opportunity International operate in many African countries. They offer small loans (e.g., 500,000 to 5,000,000 UGX) to individuals or groups. To qualify, you need a simple business plan, records of your business (even a notebook), and sometimes a group guarantee. Visit your local MFI branch and ask about 'green loans' or 'agricultural loans'. Interest rates can be high (2-5% per month), so borrow only what you can repay. Another option: government grants. Many African governments have funds for green businesses. In Uganda, the Youth Livelihood Programme (YLP) gives grants to youth groups. In Kenya, the Youth Enterprise Development Fund offers loans. In Nigeria, the Bank of Industry has a Green Energy Fund. Search online for 'government grants for briquette business [your country]'. Also check with your local district office or ministry of energy. They may have information on subsidies for briquette machines or training. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) like GVEP International, SNV, and Practical Action also provide grants or low-interest loans to clean cooking businesses. To apply, you need a clear proposal: describe your business, how much you need, what you will use it for (e.g., a new machine, raw materials), and how you will repay. Include your records to show you are serious. Attend workshops on business plan writing. Many MFIs and NGOs offer free training. Also consider crowdfunding platforms like Kiva or local savings groups (VSLA). VSLAs are common in Africa: you save with neighbors and can borrow from the group at low interest. Finally, keep your records clean. Lenders want to see that you can manage money. Even a simple cash book can help you get a loan. Start small, repay on time, and build your credit.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Business Management for Briquette and Pellet Producers

Briquette and pellet production is one of the most bankable green businesses in Africa â but only if you run it like a business, not a hobby. Whether you are pressing sawdust in Kumasi, carbonising rice husks in Kisumu, or pelletising maize cobs in Lilongwe, the difference between producers who scale and those who fold within 18 months is almost never the technology. It is the numbers. This Practical Reference gives you the working tools: how to cost a bag properly, how to price it for profit, how to keep records a lender will trust, how to survive seasonal cash flow, how to build a team, and where to find the money.

1. Calculating Costs: Raw Materials, Labour, Transport and Packaging

Your cost per bag is the foundation of everything. Split it into direct costs (they rise with every bag you make) and overheads (they exist whether you produce or not). The most common mistake African briquette producers make is forgetting transport and packaging â which together can be 20â35% of the delivered cost.

Work in a single unit: one 25 kg bag or one 50 kg bag. If you sell by kilogram, divide by the bag weight. Include:

  • Raw materials: sawdust, rice husk, maize cob, cassava peel, waste paper, binder (cassava starch, clay, molasses). If you collect free feedstock, still cost the fuel and labour to gather it.
  • Labour: piece-rate or daily wage divided by bags produced that day. Never estimate â count.
  • Transport: feedstock in (from mill or farm) + finished goods out (to market, retailer, or customer).
  • Packaging: bag, stitching, label, printing. A branded bag sells better but costs more.
  • Energy & maintenance: diesel, electricity, spare parts, lubricants.
  • Overheads: rent, licence, phone/data, depreciation on your press or pellet mill.

Worked example (25 kg bag, Kenya): raw materials KES 120; labour KES 55; transport KES 50; packaging KES 38; energy/maintenance KES 28; overheads KES 22 â total cost KES 313 per bag, or KES 12.52/kg.

2. Setting a Profitable Price per Kilogram or Bag

Price is not cost plus a random margin. Use this sequence:

  1. Know your full cost per kg.
  2. Check the market price for charcoal, firewood and competing briquettes in your town.
  3. Set a target margin of 25â40% for retail, 10â20% for wholesale/bulk.
  4. Price under charcoal if you want volume; price at parity if your briquette burns longer and cleaner â then prove it.

Formula: Price = Cost per kg Ã· (1 â Target margin %). With KES 12.52/kg cost and a 30% margin: 12.52 Ã· 0.70 = KES 17.90/kg, or about KES 448 per 25 kg bag. If local charcoal sells at KES 20/kg, you have a competitive, profitable position.

3. Keeping Simple Records: Income, Expenses and Inventory

You do not need accounting software to start. You need three books â a hardcover exercise book works fine, and a phone spreadsheet is better:

  • Cash book: every shilling in, every shilling out, dated, with a running balance.
  • Stock book: feedstock in (kg), bags produced, bags sold, bags in store. Reconcile weekly.
  • Debtors/creditors book: who owes you, whom you owe, due dates.

Record daily, not monthly. A producer who knows their numbers weekly can spot a feedstock price rise or a theft within days, not at year-end. Lenders and grant officers will ask for these records â clean books are your cheapest route to credit.

4. Managing Cash Flow When Sales Are Seasonal

In most African markets briquette demand peaks in the rainy/cold season (JuneâAugust in East Africa; NovemberâFebruary in Southern Africa) and dips in the dry/hot season when cooking moves outdoors and charcoal is cheap. Plan for the dip:

  • Build a cash reserve of 2â3 months' operating costs during peak season.
  • Buy feedstock in the off-season when sawdust and husk prices are lowest; store it dry.
  • Diversify revenue: sell to schools, restaurants, poultry farms, and institutions on contracts that smooth demand.
  • Offer off-season discounts to retailers who buy in bulk and store.
  • Stagger wages: piece-rate pay naturally falls with low production â but keep core staff.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Carbonisation and combustion hazards

Carbonising biomass in drums or kilns produces carbon monoxide â an invisible, odourless gas that kills. Never carbonise indoors, in a closed shed, or near sleeping areas. Always work outdoors or under open-sided shelter with cross-ventilation, and never sleep beside a smouldering kiln. Keep a bucket of sand and water at every kiln. Dust from sawdust and husk is explosive in enclosed spaces â wear a P2/N95 mask and eye protection when milling, mixing and bagging. Store finished briquettes away from damp and open flame. Train every worker on these rules before their first shift, and keep a written record of that training.

5. Hiring and Training Workers for Production

Start lean: 2â4 production workers, one of whom is your lead operator. Hire for reliability and physical stamina first, skills second â you can train briquette-making in a week; you cannot train punctuality.

  • Roles: feedstock collector/preparer, mixer/operator, press/mill operator, dryer/bagger, sales/loader.
  • Pay: combine a base daily rate with piece-rate per bag above a target. This aligns effort with output and protects you in low season.
  • Training: a 3-day induction covering machine safety, binder ratios, moisture control, bagging weight accuracy, and record-keeping. Refresher every 6 months.
  • Compliance: written contracts, statutory deductions (NHIF/NSSF in Kenya, NAPSA in Zambia, etc.), and a simple attendance register.
  • Retention: pay on time, provide lunch and protective gear, and give a production bonus when monthly targets are met.

6. Accessing Microfinance and Government Grants for Green Businesses

Green businesses have an advantage: climate finance, donor programmes and government agencies are actively looking for you. Prepare a one-page business profile (production capacity, monthly revenue, costs, customers, growth plan) and clean records â these unlock most doors.

  • Microfinance banks & SACCOs: offer working capital loans of USD 500â10,000. Expect 18â30% annual interest in many markets. Bring 6 months of records and a guarantor.
  • Government green funds: Kenya's Youth Enterprise Development Fund and Women Enterprise Fund; Uganda's Microfinance Support Centre; Nigeria's BOI and NESREA-linked programmes; South Africa's SEFA and IDC green funds; Ghana's MASLOC.
  • Donor & climate programmes: GIZ, SNV, WWF, UNCDF, and the Global Alliance for Clean Cookstoves network run enterprise support and matching grants.
  • Tips: apply for grants before you need them; join a producer association; register your business (sole proprietorship or Ltd) â most funds require it; and always read the repayment terms, not just the interest rate.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â I know my full cost per kg and per bag â including transport and packaging.
  • â My selling price gives at least a 25% retail margin and covers all overheads.
  • â I record every sale, expense and stock movement daily in a cash book and stock book.
  • â I hold a 2â3 month cash reserve before the low season begins.
  • â I buy and store feedstock in the off-season when prices are lowest.
  • â Every worker has a written contract and has completed safety induction.
  • â I have a one-page business profile ready for lenders and grant officers.
  • â My business is formally registered and I file statutory deductions on time.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Wood Energy for Sustainable Development (free PDF)
  • SNV â Biomass Briquette Production: A Practical Guide for Small Enterprises (free download)
  • Clean Cooking Alliance â enterprise tools, business model guides and market data
  • UNEP â reports on waste-to-energy and green enterprise finance in Africa
  • UNCDF â inclusive finance and clean energy enterprise support in Africa

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating the cost per kilogram of briquettes?
quiz.explanation: You must list all expenses to know your total costs before setting a price.

quiz.q: If raw material costs 50,000 UGX per tonne and you need 1.2 tonnes per tonne of briquettes, what is the raw material cost per kg of briquettes?
quiz.explanation: 1.2 tonnes cost 60,000 UGX, so per kg (1000 kg) it is 60 UGX.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost?
quiz.explanation: Rent is a fixed cost because it does not change with production volume.

quiz.q: If your total cost per kg is 390 UGX and you want a 30% markup, what is your selling price?
Why is it important to know your break-even point?
options: B) To know how much to sell to cover costs
C) To set the highest possible price
quiz.explanation: Break-even tells you the minimum sales needed to avoid losses.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy when setting prices compared to charcoal?
options: B) Price slightly below to attract customers
quiz.explanation: Pricing slightly below charcoal encourages customers to try briquettes.

quiz.q: Which record should you keep for every sale?
options: C) Only the total at month end
quiz.explanation: Recording date, quantity, and amount helps track income accurately.

quiz.q: What does a simple income statement show?
options: A) Total sales minus total expenses
quiz.explanation: Income statement calculates net profit by subtracting expenses from sales.

quiz.q: Why should you separate business and personal money?
options: B) To know true business profit
quiz.explanation: Mixing funds makes it impossible to know if your business is profitable.

quiz.q: How often should you do a physical inventory count?
quiz.explanation: Weekly counts help detect theft, waste, and discrepancies early.

quiz.q: What is a good way to manage cash flow during low season?
options: B) Save 20% of profit during high season
quiz.explanation: Saving during high season provides a buffer for low season expenses.

quiz.q: Which of these can help steady income year-round?
options: C) Raising prices in low season
quiz.explanation: Subscriptions provide regular, predictable income.

quiz.q: What is a cash flow budget?
options: A) A list of expected cash inflows and outflows
quiz.explanation: It helps you predict and prepare for cash shortages.

quiz.q: Why might you offer a discount during low season?
options: B) To encourage sales and keep cash coming in
quiz.explanation: Discounts can stimulate demand when sales are slow.

quiz.q: What is a key trait to look for when hiring production workers?
options: B) Reliability and willingness to learn
quiz.explanation: Reliability and trainability matter more than formal education for manual tasks.

quiz.q: What is piece-rate pay?
quiz.explanation: Piece-rate motivates productivity by paying for each unit made.

quiz.q: Why is training on safety important?
options: B) To prevent accidents and health issues
quiz.explanation: Safety training reduces injuries and long-term health problems from dust.

quiz.q: What is a good way to train new workers?
options: A) Give them a manual and leave
B) Pair them with an experienced worker
C) Let them figure it out
quiz.explanation: Buddy system provides hands-on learning and support.

quiz.q: How can you motivate sales staff?
quiz.explanation: Commission incentivizes higher sales performance.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot pay workers on time?
quiz.explanation: Early communication builds trust and allows for solutions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a microfinance institution?
quiz.explanation: BRAC is a well-known microfinance institution operating in Africa.

quiz.q: What do many MFIs require for a loan?
quiz.explanation: Even simple records show you can manage money and repay.

quiz.q: Which government program supports youth entrepreneurs in Uganda?
quiz.explanation: YLP provides grants to youth groups in Uganda.

quiz.q: What is a VSLA?
options: A) Village Savings and Loan Association
C) Voluntary Savings and Lending Authority
D) Vendor Supply and Loan Association
quiz.explanation: VSLAs are community-based savings and lending groups.

quiz.q: Why should you keep clean records when applying for a grant?
options: A) To show you are serious and can manage funds
quiz.explanation: Lenders and grantors want to see responsible financial management.

quiz.q: What is a good source of information on green grants?
quiz.explanation: District offices often have information on government and NGO programs.

quiz.q: What is crowdfunding?
options: A) Raising small amounts from many people
quiz.explanation: Crowdfunding platforms like Kiva pool small contributions.

quiz.q: What should you include in a loan application?
options: B) A clear business plan and repayment plan
quiz.explanation: A business plan shows how you will use and repay the loan.

quiz.q: Why is it important to repay loans on time?
options: A) To build credit for future loans
quiz.explanation: Timely repayment builds trust and access to larger loans.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to start building credit?
options: A) Borrow small and repay on time
quiz.explanation: Starting small and repaying builds a positive credit history.
